masthead_title: Both halves of the credit market confirmed this month's Treasury selloff for the first time — junk spreads posted their widest flag yet, and investment-grade spreads joined them today, one basis point short of the system's own test for whether that's a genuine broadening.
regime_line: High-yield credit spreads (HY OAS, the extra yield lenders demand for junk-rated debt) widened to 3.02% and posted this system's largest flag on record (z +4.14, wider than on all but a handful of days in its six-month tracking window), while investment-grade spreads (IG OAS, the same measure for highly-rated borrowers) crossed into flag territory alongside it for the first time, at 0.83% — one basis point short of the 0.84% line this system logged yesterday (CL-0025) to decide whether credit is genuinely broadening beyond high-yield or still a contained, one-market move.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — nothing due today, one claim a single basis point from confirming, a new claim opens on this morning's Core PCE

Every open conditional claim (§4B — a specific, falsifiable prediction this system logs and grades against the data, so there's a written record of what was said before the outcome was known) is checked against today's state before any new narrative is written. Yesterday is answered before today is asserted.

  • CL-0022 (whether last week's whole-curve selloff was a durable fundamental repricing, not one-day auction indigestion; due tomorrow, 2026-10-01) — unchanged, still tracking confirm. The 2-year Treasury yield closed today at 4.89%, comfortably clear of both the 4.75% confirm floor and the 4.65% refute line, with one trading day left in the window.
  • CL-0025 (whether credit is genuinely broadening from high-yield into investment-grade, or staying a contained HY-only move; due 2026-10-06) — still open, one basis point from confirming. IG OAS's freshest dated print (09-28) rose to 0.83%, up from 0.81% — a real move in the direction of confirming, but one basis point short of the 0.84% line the test requires, while HY OAS held well above its own 2.93% floor at 3.02%. Neither box closes on this print; tomorrow's dated fill is the next chance.
  • CL-0026 opens this morning — on today's Core PCE report (8:30am ET, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, consensus +0.3% m/m, up from August's +0.2%), the first hard inflation print since credit itself started confirming this month's rate story. Test: the 2-year Treasury yield (yesterday's pre-release close, 4.89%) rises 8bp or more by tomorrow's close (confirms a hot/hawkish read extending the front-end repricing); falls 8bp or more (confirms a cool/dovish read easing it); a move inside ±8bp is inconclusive and expires. Due 2026-10-01.
story_html:
The press framing this morning is still the Treasury move: CNBC and Yahoo Finance report the 10-year touched a session high above 5.29% yesterday and the 30-year climbed as high as 5.6%, a level reporting ties to 2002 for the 30-year and 2007 for the 10-year. Separately, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index fell 6.7 points to 81.9 yesterday — its lowest reading since 2014 and well short of the 89.2 economists polled by Reuters expected — which the Conference Board and Axios attribute to rising fuel costs, higher borrowing costs, and hiring anxiety.

Does this system's own data confirm that picture, or complicate it? Both, in different places. The rates side confirms cleanly: every Tier 1 Treasury tenor this system tracks is flagged again today (Dashboard, below), consistent with the multi-decade-high framing. But the equity reaction was far milder than a recap built around “record yields plus a 12-year-low confidence print” might suggest — this system's own S&P 500 close was essentially flat, down just 0.17% (Recap, above), still up 12.1% year-to-date and only 1.64% off its closing high. And the same weak-consumer headline sits awkwardly next to Carnival's earnings this week: a beat-and-raise quarter with record customer deposits (Movers, below) — a live, testable version of the “survey versus revealed spending” question this system flags rather than resolves. What's genuinely new since yesterday's brief is credit: investment-grade spreads joined high-yield in flag territory for the first time (Dashboard, Claims, above), one basis point short of this system's own test for whether that's a real broadening. Oil, meanwhile, eased rather than extended — WTI fell 3.5% to $89.38, consistent with CL-0024's refutation two days ago that the weekend Iran/Houthi headlines would produce a durable supply-risk premium.

dashboard_interp_html:
Every Treasury tenor this system tracks is flagged again and moved further today: the 3-month bill to 4.25% (z +2.93), the 2-year to 4.89% (z +2.76), the 10-year to 5.26% (z +3.17), and the 30-year to 5.59% (z +3.10). The 10-year real yield (what a bond actually pays after inflation) sits at 2.90% as of its 09-28 dated print (z +2.81), while the 10-year breakeven (the bond market's own inflation forecast) is flat at 2.34% the same day, essentially unflagged (z +0.10) — the real-rate side is still doing almost all of the work, not a fresh inflation scare, the same read this system has made for weeks.

Credit just became the loudest thing on this dashboard. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies) rose to 3.02% as of its 09-28 dated print — up 9bp on the day and 36bp over five sessions — and now carries this system's single largest flag of any series, at any point, since tracking began (z +4.14). IG OAS (the same measure for highly-rated companies) ticked up 2bp to 0.83% and crossed into flag territory for the first time (z +1.97) — a real move, but one basis point short of the 0.84% line CL-0025 set to call it a genuine broadening rather than an HY-only story (Claims, above). SOFR (the overnight bank-funding rate) stayed at 3.90% (z +3.88) — still elevated but the same aging, already-resolved mechanical story (CL-0020) as the Fed's rate hike six weeks ago working through the 120-day comparison window, not new information. The curve stayed right-side up: 2s10s at +37bp (z -0.62, no inversion) and 3m10y at +101bp, still flagged (z +2.40) as the front end keeps repricing faster than the long end.

Why this matters: this is the environment setting new mortgage-rate quotes, CD and money-market yields, and the discount rate bond funds mark their holdings against every day. And today's move is the first time both the junk and investment-grade slices of the corporate-lending market are pricing in a little more risk at the same time — not yet a large move in absolute terms (both spreads are still far below where they sat in March, per this system's own history), but a real change in direction that, if it continues, shows up as tighter or pricier financing for ordinary businesses, not just a bond-market number.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 16 name candidates and 0 sector divergences qualified today; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note.

Fair Isaac (FICO) −26.52% (617.87, from 840.89) — what happened: the day's single largest move in the entire scan, by a wide margin. Stated reason: GuruFocus and Yahoo Finance report FHFA Director Bill Pulte announced Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will move to a unified mortgage-pricing model incorporating VantageScore — ending FICO's decades-long position as the only credit score the two mortgage giants accept — while TransUnion said it will hold standalone VantageScore 4.0 mortgage pricing at $0.99 per score through 2028. Reporting says the news rattled the whole credit-bureau sector: TransUnion fell 4%, Equifax 6.7%, and London-listed Experian 1.2%. Read-through: idiosyncratic — a regulatory shock to the credit-scoring industry's structure, not a macro signal. The one adjacent, real-world point worth flagging: this is a mortgage-market-plumbing change, not a rate or credit-availability one — it doesn't show up in this system's own rate or spread series.

Carnival (CCL) +13.41% (25.11, from 22.14) — what happened: the sharpest gain in the scan. Stated reason: GuruFocus reports an all-time-high net income of $1.9 billion, an EPS beat, record third-quarter customer deposits (up nearly 7% year over year on flat capacity), and a raised full-year adjusted-EPS outlook to roughly $2.24. Read-through: a direct, earnings-verified data point on high-end discretionary consumer spending — and it sits awkwardly next to yesterday's 12-year-low consumer-confidence survey (Story, above). Royal Caribbean (RCL, +7.45%) moved the same day on its own catalyst — a $3B Sandals resorts stake and analyst upgrades citing “very strong travel spending” — corroborating evidence, not the same story, but pointing the same direction: booked travel demand looks stronger than the confidence survey does.

Bloom Energy (BE) +10.80% (291.25, from 262.87) — what happened: a near-complete reversal of Monday's slide. Stated reason: Motley Fool and TradingKey report RBC Capital reaffirmed its Outperform rating and $335 price target after Monday's close, and Oracle reaffirmed its commitment to the multi-gigawatt Project Jupiter fuel-cell data-center deal — the same underlying financing item this system has flagged for several sessions running — even though the project's force-majeure/permit-delay concern remains formally unresolved per that same reporting. Read-through: the clearest AI-capex/financing-cycle read-through of the day — the physical-power layer of the AI buildout, and a live, still-unresolved financing thread this system keeps tracking. → Route to NR commentary process: plausibly relevant to AI-capex/financing-cycle thesis monitoring; no position-level view expressed.

No sector note today: the mechanical scan found zero GICS sector ETFs diverging 1.5 percentage points or more from the S&P.

tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (this system's chip-fund proxy for AI capex) outperformed SPY today, +1.15% vs. -0.18%, a +1.33pp gap on a broad-based chip and equipment rally — Applied Materials (+5.19%), Marvell (+4.51%), Lumentum (+5.66%), Corning (+4.70%), KLA (+3.89%), Lam Research (+2.99%), Oracle (+3.91%), and Meta (+3.24%) all traded up, none individually clearing this system's mechanical movers threshold on their own but collectively pointing the same direction as Bloom Energy's move (Movers, above). None of the individually smaller moves get their own mover slot — the mechanical cap exists precisely so a broad, correlated sector day doesn't crowd out the three most decision-relevant single-name stories.

Financing watch: Bloom Energy's Project Jupiter thread (Movers, above) remains the live item — Oracle's own reaffirmation moved the stock today, but the underlying force-majeure/permit-delay concern this system flagged last week has not been formally resolved by either party per today's reporting. This system's own IG OAS reading (Dashboard, above) crossed into flag territory for the first time today, which is a broad, market-wide signal, not an AI-specific one — but it is happening on top of a month of Treasury yields at multi-decade highs, which is exactly the environment in which a fast-growing, debt-hungry issuer class (hyperscalers and their vendors) gets priced more cautiously before the broad aggregate does.

Why this matters: this is the layer of the AI story that doesn't show up in a single day's stock move — who is financing the buildout, and at what price — and it is the piece Unit 7 of this curriculum (financing cycles and reflexivity, not yet reached) will eventually give a formal framework for reading against the Lucent reference class.

Looking ahead: no fresh hyperscaler capex-guidance update beyond the items above. → Route to NR commentary process: Bloom Energy's Project Jupiter item remains an open, plausibly relevant thread for AI-capex/financing-cycle thesis monitoring; no position-level view expressed (§8).
calendar_note_html: A heavy data morning: ADP private payrolls (consensus 70K, prior 38K) and Core PCE (consensus +0.3% m/m, up from +0.2%, the Fed's own preferred inflation gauge) both land at 8:30am ET alongside Final Q3 GDP (consensus 1.5%, unchanged) and personal income/spending. Chicago PMI follows at 9:45am. Four Fed officials speak later today — Barkin, Cook, Goolsbee, and Kashkari. Why this matters to the current regime: with every Tier 1 rate series flagged and both credit gauges now confirming (Dashboard, Claims, above), Core PCE is the first hard inflation data point since credit itself started moving — a hot print would reinforce the whole-curve story already in motion; a cool one would be the first data-based case for relief, tested against tomorrow's 2-year close and the next breakeven fill (CL-0026, Claims, above) rather than against today's headline reaction alone.
concept_title: QT versus the TGA drain — two ways to shrink reserves that look identical in the reserves identity but mean different things
concept_html: Segment 3's identity said reserves ≈ the Fed's balance sheet minus the TGA minus the ON RRP — and showed a big TGA build (from a Treasury refunding) draining reserves without the Fed doing anything. But there's a second way reserves shrink: the Fed's own balance-sheet runoff, often called quantitative tightening or QT, where the Fed lets bonds mature without buying new ones to replace them. Both show up as the same falling number in the identity; they are not the same event. A TGA-driven drain is temporary and mechanical — the cash sits in the government's account until it's spent back out, and reserves refill. A QT-driven drain is the Fed's own deliberate, ongoing policy choice, and it doesn't refill on its own. This week's own numbers (Dashboard, above, all thin history) show which one is actually happening right now: the Fed's balance sheet itself barely moved, +$1.156 billion week over week, while the TGA alone moved nearly a hundred times that, +$100.056 billion. This week's reserve pressure is almost entirely the Treasury's doing, not the Fed actively shrinking its balance sheet — a distinction that matters because one of these reverses itself in weeks and the other doesn't reverse until the Fed decides to stop it.
client_translation: When the news says the Fed is "still doing QT," that's a separate, slower story from a big Treasury bond sale temporarily soaking up cash from the banking system — and this week, the numbers say it's almost entirely the second one, which tends to ease up on its own once the government spends that cash back out.
client_lens_html:
“My credit score company's stock just dropped 26% — is something wrong with FICO scores, or my mortgage?” Likely to come up given the size of the move and the brand recognition (Movers, above). No — this is a change to how Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac price a fee they charge lenders, opening the door to a rival credit-score provider (VantageScore) alongside FICO, not a change to how credit scores themselves work or a statement about mortgage credit quality.

“I keep hearing consumers are struggling, but Carnival just posted record earnings — which one is true?” A natural question given both stories broke within a day of each other (Story, Movers, above). Both, in different slices of the same economy: survey-based confidence measures how people say they feel, which fell to a 12-year low on fuel prices and hiring anxiety; actual bookings and spending, at least in cruise and travel, came in at record levels. The gap between how people say they feel and what they actually do with their money is exactly the kind of thing this system flags rather than resolves for you.

“If today's inflation report comes in hot, does that mean rates keep climbing and my bond funds keep losing value?” Timely given Core PCE lands this morning (Calendar, above). Directionally yes if it's hot and the market reads it that way — a hot print would tend to push yields higher, which is a further mark-to-market hit for existing bond funds, unchanged mechanics from every prior week this system has covered. What's different to watch for this time: whether it's the first print to actually move the bond market's own inflation forecast (the breakeven, which has sat flat all month), versus just adding to the same real-rate story that's been driving the move so far — a distinction this system will test explicitly (CL-0026, Claims, above) rather than call from the headline alone.
